# Design review: assembly and parting-out findings

Found while building the step-by-step animated assembly guide (`steps.yaml`) and sweeping every
motion through the CAD (`check_paths.py`). Each finding says what made that step harder than it
needed to be, the recommendation, and what was done. **Status:** *done* = the CAD, PCB, BOM and
guide now follow the recommendation; *guide updated* = the old written procedure could not be
followed as written, and the guide now shows an order that works.

## F1

**Bushing alignment procedure can't be followed as written**

Impact: high · Status: done · Area: Movement plates (§1)

**Observation.** The old §1 said to screw P1 and P2 together, drop all 13 bushings in "until they touch the
surface", then slide the sensor and knob shafts and arbor I "through both plates" while the 638
is wet. With the plates stacked neither is on a flat surface, and every sensor and knob shaft's
collar is wider than the bushing bore, so the shafts can only go in from P1's side before P2.

**Recommendation.** Align with plain drill blanks, exactly the shaft diameters, slid through both plates from above.

**Resolution.** Each plate's bushings are glued flat on glass (chamfer down), the frame is screwed together on its
standoffs, and three 1/8" and three 5/32" drill blanks (`align_pin_*`, in the tool list) line the
pairs up while the 638 cures (§1.5–1.6). The shafts are fitted once.

Seen in: 1.5 Glue the bushings into P1 and P2; 1.6 Line up the bushing pairs with drill blanks

## F2

**Nothing held the crystal and spiders while the shell was turned over and lowered**

Impact: high · Status: done · Area: Upper shell (§8)

**Observation.** The crystal, frame spider and seat spider were loaded into the shell upside down and only clamped
once the four top screws reached the hand standoffs, so they had to be held while the shell was
turned over and lowered over the thumbwheels.

**Recommendation.** Retain the spider stack to the shell independently of the top screws.

**Resolution.** First fixed with two M1.6 screws through the top face and both spiders. The simplicity review
([DESIGN_REVIEW.md](../DESIGN_REVIEW.md) S3) then removed the spiders altogether: the crystal is
glued to a 2 mm land under the top face like a watch crystal, so the shell is one piece when it is
turned over, the top face rests directly on the hand standoffs (now the same M2×8 part as the
gear standoffs), and the two screws, two nuts, two spiders and their countersinks are gone.

Seen in: 8.1 Upper shell, upside down; 8.2 Turn the shell back over

## F3

**The motor mesh was set by solder-joint play, using the carrier as a jig**

Impact: high · Status: done · Area: Movement (§4, §6)

**Observation.** Setting the X27 mesh took five jig steps (bay standoffs on the bare carrier, P1, arbors, X27,
solder its sockets from below, pull it out again), although the only adjustment was the socket
pins' play in their holes.

**Recommendation.** Rely on the designed centre distance and solder the X27 sockets with the other sockets.

**Resolution.** The X27 sockets are soldered in §4.1; the jig steps are gone. The motor pair has the same
backlash as the other gear-to-gear pairs: its needle gear is cut loose enough to run at a
worst-case cut, with a tight `_T` alternate if it is sloppy (§6.6 test).

Seen in: 4.1 Populate the carrier; 6.6 X27 in through P1's opening

## F9

**The motor gear can't pass P1's opening, so the movement can't be finished on the bench**

Impact: high · Status: guide updated · Area: Movement and case (§5, §6)

**Observation.** The old guide lowered the finished movement onto the carrier "with the X27 and its gear rising up
through P1's opening". The 34T motor gear (Ø28.8 mm, offset from the motor body) is wider than the
slot, and the hand gears have to pass the motor gear's level.

**Recommendation.** Fit the frame into the case first, then the X27 through its opening, then P2, dial and hands.

**Resolution.** That is the order in §6 and §7. With F3 there is no jig to pull the X27 out of; the X27 is only
lifted out for servicing.

Seen in: 6.6 X27 in through P1's opening

## F10

**The crown stem blocks the carrier if the crown goes in first**

Impact: medium · Status: guide updated · Area: Case (§6)

**Observation.** The crown stem's inner end reaches about 1 mm inside the carrier outline at switch height, so the
board can't be lowered past an installed crown.

**Recommendation.** Fit the carrier first, then the crown and its E-clip.

**Resolution.** §6.1 and §6.2 are in that order.

Seen in: 6.1 Carrier into the lower tray; 6.2 Crown

## F4

**P2 had to find seven shaft tips at once**

Impact: medium · Status: done · Area: Movement (§6)

**Observation.** All shaft tips ended at P2's top face, with 0.08 mm clearance in the bushings, so P2 had to be
coaxed onto all of them together.

**Recommendation.** Lead-in chamfers on the tips and bushing bores, and knob shafts slightly longer.

**Resolution.** The turned kit specifies a 0.2 mm × 45° chamfer on every shaft tip and on one end of every bushing
bore (fitted chamfer down), and the knob shafts stand 0.6 mm proud of P2 so it picks them up first.
Sensor shafts stay flush: the needle sweeps 0.45 mm above them.

Seen in: 6.7 Lower P2 onto the shaft tips

## F5

**Speaker and mic leads were soldered in with the movement dangling beside the tray**

Impact: medium · Status: done · Area: Electronics (§5, §6)

**Observation.** The leads were soldered to J5/J4 with the finished movement standing beside the tray, and had to be
desoldered to lift the movement out.

**Recommendation.** Put connectors on both leads.

**Resolution.** J4 and J5 are Molex PicoBlade 53047 vertical headers (5 and 2 pins) on the carrier, at the same
places, rerouted with 0 DRC violations. The leads are pre-crimped pigtails soldered at the mic and
speaker on the bench, and plug in before the frame goes down (§6.4).

Seen in: 4.1 Populate the carrier; 5.4 Speaker; 5.5 Microphone under P2; 6.4 Plug in the speaker and mic leads

## F6

**Six hinge holes were hand-drilled through the finished case**

Impact: medium · Status: done · Area: Hinge (§3, §8)

**Observation.** The shell and lid came without hinge holes and were drilled on the bench through a drill guide
hooked over the closed case: the riskiest moment in the build.

**Recommendation.** Laser-cut the holes in the case blanks and drill only the leaf.

**Resolution.** The holes are laser-cut in the shell and lid walls. The hinge is drilled flat on the bench through
`hinge_gauge`, which also checks its cut and trim (§3.7); the hooked drill guide is gone. The hinge
is screwed to the lid first, while both sides can be reached.

Seen in: 3.7 Hinge: check it and drill the leaves

## F7

**The hinge was cut from 72-inch stock by hand**

Impact: low · Status: done · Area: Parting out (§0, §3)

**Observation.** Guden sells the brass hinge in 72" lengths, and the guide had you cut a five-knuckle piece with a
Dremel, stake the pin and file the lid leaf to a scribed line.

**Recommendation.** Ask Guden to supply it cut and trimmed.

**Resolution.** The BOM asks Guden for one 63.5 mm piece, both end knuckles on the fixed leaf, pin staked, lid leaf
trimmed to 5.6 mm from the pivot, quoted with the §0 sample. The gauge checks it; cutting it
yourself remains a fallback.

Seen in: 3.7 Hinge: check it and drill the leaves

## F8

**The crown corner was held by a loose nut**

Impact: low · Status: done · Area: Chassis (§1, §8)

**Observation.** The fourth gear standoff ended in a loose M2 nut held under P1 with tweezers, right above the crown
switch, in the corner that takes the crown presses.

**Recommendation.** Replace the nut with a short M2×4 F-F standoff; check the corner on the prototype.

**Resolution.** `standoff_corner` (M2×4 F-F, 0.6 mm above the crown switch) replaces the nut. A fourth floor post
still has no room past the crown switch; §8.7 tests the corner's stiffness on the prototype.

Seen in: 1.6 Line up the bushing pairs with drill blanks
